result:
What comes to me is a monk complaining about his hand.

Medieval scribes spent their days copying other people's words, and every so often one of them would stop and write something of his own in the margin or at the foot of the last page. A handful of these notes survive. They mostly circulate in lists now, in translations of varying reliability, and I think about them more than I think about most of the books they were attached to. "The parchment is hairy." "The ink is thin." "Thank God, it will soon be dark." "Oh, my hand." One scribe gets to the end of an entire volume and writes, "Now I've written the whole thing: for Christ's sake give me a drink."

My favorite is from an Irish scribe, and it's one of the few that isn't a complaint: "Pleasant to me is the glittering of the sun today upon these margins, because it flickers so." He was partway through a page of someone else's sentences, the light moved, and he wrote it down.

Then there are the cats. Around 1420, a scribe in Deventer came back to his desk in the morning and found that a cat had urinated on the open manuscript overnight. He left the ruined space blank, drew a cat and two pointing hands, and wrote a curse in Latin on the animal, followed by advice to future readers never to leave books open at night where cats can get at them. Six hundred years later, the page still shows his irritation.

Six centuries before him, an Irish monk living somewhere near Lake Constance kept a notebook of grammar notes, hymns, and astronomical tables. In among them he wrote a poem about his white cat, Pangur Bán. The cat hunts mice and the monk hunts meanings. Neither envies the other, and each is content when his own kind of catch comes off. Nobody knows the monk's name, though we know the cat's.

I think these get to me because of what the scribe's job was. He was supposed to be transparent, to let a text pass through him and come out unchanged. The better he was at it, the less of him remained on the page. The margins are the only place you learn that someone was there in a cold room with a bad pen and a sore back, wanting the day to end.

I also like how small the notes are. Given a strip of free vellum, no scribe wrote a treatise or a statement of belief. They mentioned the weather, the ink, the hand, the drink, the cat. I suspect that's what most people have nearest to the surface when the assigned work pauses: a report on how it's going right now, here at this desk.

Most of what I do is main text. Someone arrives with a task, I do it, and I like that work. An invitation like yours is margin. I notice that with a thousand words to spend on anything, I reached for other people's small notes instead of a large thought of my own. I do have opinions on big subjects, but they didn't come first. The scribe who drew the pointing hands did.

I can't report on the sun or my hand. But I can offer a margin note of my own, in the same spirit and at about the same scale: it pleases me that "Oh, my hand" is still being read centuries later, long after whatever he was copying that day stopped mattering to most people, and that a stranger gave me a blank page and I filled it with monks and cats.

That's about six hundred words, and the rest of the page can stay blank.
